claim: Starved flies exhibit enhanced sensitivity to attractive odors.
source: Starved flies exhibit enhanced sensitivity to attractive odors and reduced sensitivity to aversive odors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Starved flies exhibit reduced sensitivity to aversive odors.
source: Starved flies exhibit enhanced sensitivity to attractive odors and reduced sensitivity to aversive odors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Functional remodeling of the olfactory map is mediated by two parallel neuromodulatory systems.
source: Here, we show that a functional remodeling of the olfactory map is mediated by two parallel neuromodulatory systems that act in opposing directions on olfactory attraction and aversion at the level of the first synapse.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Short neuropeptide F sensitizes an antennal lobe glomerulus wired for attraction.
source: Short neuropeptide F sensitizes an antennal lobe glomerulus wired for attraction, while tachykinin (DTK) suppresses activity of a glomerulus wired for aversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Tachykinin (DTK) suppresses activity of a glomerulus wired for aversion.
source: Short neuropeptide F sensitizes an antennal lobe glomerulus wired for attraction, while tachykinin (DTK) suppresses activity of a glomerulus wired for aversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Parallel neuromodulatory systems functionally reconfigure early olfactory processing to optimize detection of nutrients at the risk of ignoring potentially toxic food resources.
source: Thus we show parallel neuromodulatory systems functionally reconfigure early olfactory processing to optimize detection of nutrients at the risk of ignoring potentially toxic food resources.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sensory systems undergo dramatic functional modifications when animals enter different internal states such as hunger or arousal.
source: Sensory systems undergo dramatic functional modifications when animals enter different internal states such as hunger or arousal (Su and Wang, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neuromodulators are an important class of molecules positioned to exert significant influence over local neural circuits through their effects on neuronal excitability and network properties.
source: Neuromodulators are an important class of molecules positioned to exert significant influence over local neural circuits through their effects on neuronal excitability and network properties (Bargmann and Marder, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Dopamine, short neuropeptide F (sNPF) and NPF have been demonstrated to influence different aspects of appetitive behaviors such as taste sensitivity.
source: Neuromodulators such as dopamine, short neuropeptide F (sNPF) and NPF have been demonstrated to influence different aspects of appetitive behaviors such as taste sensitivity (Inagaki et al., 2012; Marella et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014), the formation and expression of appetitive memories (Krashes et al., 2009), odor preference (Root et al., 2011; Beshel and Zhong, 2013), and control of food intake (Lee et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Food deprivation increases an animal's tolerance for noxious stimuli.
source: For example, food deprivation increases an animal's tolerance for noxious stimuli (Gillette et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2005; Inagaki et al., 2014) and suppresses escape behavior at the risk of predation (Gillette et al., 2000; Gaudry and Kristan, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Food deprivation suppresses escape behavior at the risk of predation.
source: For example, food deprivation increases an animal's tolerance for noxious stimuli (Gillette et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2005; Inagaki et al., 2014) and suppresses escape behavior at the risk of predation (Gillette et al., 2000; Gaudry and Kristan, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Starvation heightens sensitivity in odorant receptor neurons (ORNs) that are critical for behavioral attraction to appetitive odors through neuromodulatory mechanisms.
source: In Drosophila, starvation heightens sensitivity in odorant receptor neurons (ORNs) that are critical for behavioral attraction to appetitive odors through neuromodulatory mechanisms (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Starvation has been shown to reduce behavioral avoidance to innately aversive odors.
source: Starvation has also been shown to reduce behavioral avoidance to innately aversive odors (Bracker et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The starvation effect on reducing behavioral avoidance to aversive odors requires the presence of appetitive odors and has been suggested to occur at higher order levels of the Drosophila brain.
source: This starvation effect requires the presence of appetitive odors and has been suggested to occur at higher order levels of the Drosophila brain (Bracker et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Activation of the DM1 glomerulus, innervated by Or42b ORNs, triggers attraction to an odor.
source: In particular, activation of the DM1 glomerulus, innervated by Or42b ORNs, triggers attraction to an odor, while activation of DM5, innervated by Or85a ORNs, reduces attraction to high concentrations of vinegar (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Activation of DM5, innervated by Or85a ORNs, reduces attraction to high concentrations of vinegar.
source: In particular, activation of the DM1 glomerulus, innervated by Or42b ORNs, triggers attraction to an odor, while activation of DM5, innervated by Or85a ORNs, reduces attraction to high concentrations of vinegar (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Activity in DM1 and DM5 represents positive and negative valence, respectively.
source: Thus, activity in DM1 and DM5 represents positive and negative valence, respectively, and physiological modulation of these glomeruli should alter olfactory behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited work on DM1 and DM5 function.

claim: At intermediate concentrations, food odors such as vinegar are attractive to hungry flies.
source: At intermediate concentrations, food odors such as vinegar are attractive to hungry flies. At low or high concentrations, however, odors are ignored (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009; Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At low or high concentrations, food odors are ignored by flies.
source: At intermediate concentrations, food odors such as vinegar are attractive to hungry flies. At low or high concentrations, however, odors are ignored (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009; Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In starved flies, the appetitive index rises (from 23 to 60) as the vinegar concentration increases (0.5–25%), but then steadily declines at higher concentrations.
source: In starved flies, the appetitive index rises (from 23 to 60) as the vinegar concentration increases (0.5–25%), but then steadily declines at higher concentrations (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At all tested concentrations (0.5–100%), the appetitive index in starved flies is greater than that of the fed flies.
source: At all tested concentrations (0.5–100%), the appetitive index in starved flies is greater than that of the fed flies.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: sNPF enhances the olfactory sensitivity of ORNs and increases appetitive behavior at low odor concentrations.
source: sNPF, a Drosophila homolog of the mammalian orexigenic neuropeptide Y (NPY) (Barsh and Schwartz, 2002; Lee et al., 2004), enhances the olfactory sensitivity of ORNs and increases appetitive behavior at low odor concentrations (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: At low concentrations (0.5–1%) of cider vinegar, knockdown of sNPFR eliminated the behavioral difference between starved and fed flies.
source: At low concentrations (0.5–1%) of cider vinegar, knockdown of sNPFR eliminated the behavioral difference between starved and fed flies (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At high concentrations (5–25%) of cider vinegar, the appetitive index of sNPFR knockdown flies remains significantly higher than that of the control fed flies.
source: However, at high concentrations (5–25%), the appetitive index of sNPFR knockdown flies remains significantly higher than that of the control fed flies.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In a fed state, sNPFR knockdown had no behavioral effect compared to the control flies.
source: In a fed state, sNPFR knockdown had no behavioral effect compared to the control flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A small increase in GPCR expression can have a dramatic effect on neural circuit function and related behavior.
source: Most neuromodulators signal through G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Greengard, 2001) and a small increase in GPCR expression can have a dramatic effect on neural circuit function and related behavior (Bendesky et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified 34 GPCRs that have higher expression in the antennae of starved flies.
source: This analysis identified 34 GPCRs that have higher expression in the antennae of starved flies (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: sNPFR is upregulated in the antennae of starved flies.
source: This group included sNPFR, a GPCR we had previously shown to undergo upregulation in Or42b ORNs after starvation (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by both the current RNA-seq data and a citation to previous work.

claim: Dopamine 2-like and dopamine-ecdysone receptors are upregulated in the antennae of starved flies and have been implicated in enhancing fly sugar receptor sensitivity in the starved state.
source: Other upregulated GPCRs, not yet described in ORNs, include the dopamine 2-like and dopamine-ecdysone receptors which have both been implicated in enhancing fly sugar receptor sensitivity in the starved state (Inagaki et al., 2012; Marella et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data and citations to previous work.

claim: Starved DTKR knockdown flies do not behave differently from control starved flies in response to low concentrations (0.5–1%) of cider vinegar.
source: Starved DTKR knockdown flies do not behave differently from control starved flies in response to low concentrations (0.5–1%) of cider vinegar.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The appetitive index of starved DTKR knockdown flies at high concentrations (5–25%) of cider vinegar is significantly lower than that of control flies.
source: In contrast, their appetitive index at high concentrations (5–25%) of cider vinegar is significantly lower than that of control flies (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DTKR knockdown has no effect on the behavior of fed flies.
source: Furthermore, we found no effect of DTKR knockdown on the behavior of fed flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DTKR signaling is necessary for starvation-dependent change in food search behavior at high, but not low odor concentrations.
source: Thus, DTKR signaling is necessary for starvation-dependent change in food search behavior at high, but not low odor concentrations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on DTKR knockdown effects.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of the sNPF peptide and DTKR in Orco neurons abolished the effect of starvation, leading to behavior indistinguishable from that of fed flies.
source: Indeed, simultaneous knockdown of the sNPF peptide (the equivalent of sNFPR knockdown, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and DTKR in Orco neurons abolished the effect of starvation, leading to behavior indistinguishable from that of fed flies (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both sNPFR and DTKR modulation systems are required to bring about the appetitive behavior observed in starved flies.
source: Thus, these two modulation systems are both required to bring about the appetitive behavior observed in starved flies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the double knockdown experimental data.

claim: Starvation suppresses olfactory sensitivity of DM5, a glomerulus that mediates aversion.
source: Strikingly, starvation suppresses olfactory sensitivity of DM5 (Figure 2B) a glomerulus that mediates aversion (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2B, with the functional role of DM5 supported by citation.

claim: DM5 is the only glomerulus recruited by vinegar that is modulated by starvation at high odor intensity.
source: Furthermore, DM5 is the only glomerulus recruited by vinegar that is modulated by starvation at high odor intensity (see Figure 2—source data 1 for a more complete characterization of glomerular responses to vinegar in fed and starved flies).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: DM5 became activated at 20% saturated vapor (SV pressure) in fed flies, but not until 80% SV in starved flies.
source: Testing a range of concentrations, we found that DM5 became activated at 20% saturated vapor (SV pressure) in fed flies, but not until 80% SV in starved flies (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At the concentrations when DM5 is suppressed by starvation, DM1 responses saturate and do not exhibit further modulation by starvation.
source: At the concentrations when DM5 is suppressed by starvation, DM1 responses saturate and do not exhibit further modulation by starvation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Knockdown of DTKR in ORNs abolished the starvation-dependent suppression in DM5 across a range of odor concentrations.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, knockdown of DTKR in ORNs abolished the starvation-dependent suppression in DM5 across a range of odor concentrations (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Starvation-dependent sensitization in DM1 was abolished by knockdown of sNPFR.
source: Furthermore, starvation-dependent sensitization in DM1 was abolished by knockdown of sNPFR (Figure 2D), as previously reported (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2D, with support from a citation to previous work.

claim: The response of DM5 PNs to ethyl butyrate is modulated by DTKR.
source: We next asked whether the starvation modulation of DM5 generalizes to other odors, and found that the response of DM5 PNs to ethyl butyrate is similarly modulated by DTKR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: A population of GABAergic local interneurons (LNs) labeled by the GH298-Gal4 line is immunoreactive for DTK.
source: Previous studies have shown that a population of GABAergic local interneurons (LNs) labeled by the GH298-Gal4 line is immunoreactive for DTK (Ignell et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: DTK peptide knockdown in LNs abolished the starvation-dependent DM5 suppression.
source: Imaging DM5 responses to cider vinegar, we found that DTK peptide knockdown in LNs abolished the starvation-dependent DM5 suppression, whereas expression of DTK-RNAi in ORNs did not have any effect (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of DTK-RNAi in LNs, but not ORNs, significantly reduces the appetitive index for food search behavior.
source: Next, we asked if DTK expression in LNs is required for starvation-dependent behavior, and found expression of DTK-RNAi in LNs, but not ORNs, significantly reduces the appetitive index for food search behavior (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DTKR signaling is required for the starvation-induced suppression of DM5, which augments food search behavior.
source: Together, these studies demonstrate that DTKR signaling is required for the starvation-induced suppression of DM5, which augments food search behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on DTK and DTKR.

claim: Exogenous sNPF increased the response of DM1 but not DM5 in starved flies.
source: We found that exogenous sNPF increased the response of DM1 but not DM5 in starved flies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Exogenous DTK suppressed activity in DM5 but not DM1 in starved flies.
source: Conversely, exogenous DTK suppressed activity in DM5 but not DM1 in starved flies (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DM1 and DM5 appear to be specifically sensitive to the addition of sNPF and DTK, respectively, in both a glomerular-specific and starvation-dependent manner.
source: Thus, DM1 and DM5 appear to be specifically sensitive to the addition of sNPF and DTK, respectively, in both a glomerular-specific and starvation-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the peptide application experiments.

claim: Knockdown of sNPFR in Or42b neurons abolished starvation-dependent sensitization in DM1.
source: Knockdown of sNPFR in Or42b neurons abolished starvation-dependent sensitization in DM1 (Figure 4C) and reduced the appetitive index to the same extent as when the RNAi construct was expressed in most ORNs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging and behavioral data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Knockdown of DTKR in Or85a neurons abolished starvation-dependent suppression of DM5.
source: Likewise, knockdown of DTKR in Or85a neurons abolished starvation-dependent suppression of DM5 and reduced food finding to the same extent as when the RNAi construct was expressed in most ORNs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging and behavioral data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: sNPF and DTK modulate distinct ORNs in opposite directions, in what appears to be a push–pull optimization strategy to increase the attractive valence of an odor.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that sNPF and DTK modulate distinct ORNs in opposite directions, in what appears to be a push–pull optimization strategy to increase the attractive valence of an odor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the glomerulus-specific knockdown experiments.

claim: Targeted expression of NaChBac in Or42b neurons increased the olfactory sensitivity of DM1 in fed flies and resulted in a marked increase in appetitive index.
source: Targeted expression of NaChBac in Or42b neurons increased the olfactory sensitivity of DM1 in fed flies and resulted in a marked increase in appetitive index (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging and behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Expression of NaChBac in Or85a neurons increased activity of DM5 in starved flies and was accompanied by a significant decrease in appetitive index.
source: Likewise, expression of NaChBac in Or85a neurons increased activity of DM5 in starved flies and was accompanied by a significant decrease in appetitive index (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging and behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Insulin signaling has been implicated in mediating differences between rover and sitter, naturally occurring polymorphisms in the foraging gene that lead to dramatic differences in feeding behaviors.
source: Previous work has implicated insulin signaling in mediating differences between rover and sitter, naturally occurring polymorphisms in the foraging gene that lead to dramatic differences in feeding behaviors (de Belle et al., 1989; Kent et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Insulin negatively regulates sNPFR gene expression in DM1 ORNs.
source: We also recently reported that insulin negatively regulates sNPFR gene expression in DM1 ORNs (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Flies fed with sugar and wortmannin exhibited a suppressed DM5 response that was accompanied by an increased appetitive index, thereby mimicking the starved state.
source: Flies fed with sugar and wortmannin exhibited a suppressed DM5 response that was accompanied by an increased appetitive index (Figure 5A), thereby mimicking the starved state.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging and behavioral data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The suppression of DM5 by wortmannin occurs through increased DTKR signaling, because targeted knockdown of DTKR in ORNs blocked the effect of wortmannin.
source: Moreover, this suppression occurs through increased DTKR signaling, because targeted knockdown of DTKR in ORNs blocked the effect of wortmannin.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging and behavioral data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ectopic expression of a constitutively active InR (InR-CA) in Or85a neurons of starved flies led to increased DM5 activity and decreased appetitive behavior, thereby mimicking satiety.
source: Indeed, ectopic expression of a constitutively active InR (InR-CA) in Or85a neurons of starved flies led to increased DM5 activity and decreased appetitive behavior (Figure 5B), thereby mimicking satiety.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging and behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Insulin signaling in Or85a neurons gates the expression of DTKR to modulate DM5 activity and appetitive behavior.
source: Thus, insulin signaling in Or85a neurons gates the expression of DTKR to modulate DM5 activity and appetitive behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the insulin signaling manipulation experiments.

claim: Starvation does not simply scale up or down global activity in the antennal lobe.
source: We show here that starvation does not simply scale up or down global activity in the antennal lobe.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that different glomeruli are modulated in opposite directions.

claim: Starvation upregulates activity in certain sensory channels and downregulates it in others in what appears to be an optimization strategy that may serve to increase the hedonic value of food odors.
source: Rather, it upregulates activity in certain sensory channels and downregulates it in others in what appears to be an optimization strategy that may serve to increase the hedonic value of food odors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential modulation of DM1 and DM5.

claim: Individual neurons may read the same global metabolic signals and differentially respond in a manner that fine tunes local circuits towards a concerted modulation of appetitive behaviors.
source: Thus, individual neurons may read the same global metabolic signals and differentially respond in a manner that fine tunes local circuits towards a concerted modulation of appetitive behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the observation that insulin signaling affects both DM1 and DM5 but in opposite directions.

claim: Starved flies exhibit enhanced odor sensitivity in ORNs that mediate behavioral attraction and decreased sensitivity in ORNs that mediate behavioral aversion.
source: Here we demonstrate that shifts in the internal metabolic state of an animal lead to dramatic functional changes in its olfactory circuit and behaviors. Starved flies exhibit enhanced odor sensitivity in ORNs that mediate behavioral attraction and decreased sensitivity in ORNs that mediate behavioral aversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: sNPFR signaling increases sensitivity in Or42b ORNs and thus enhances behavioral attraction.
source: In our earlier study, we showed that sNPFR signaling increases sensitivity in Or42b ORNs and thus enhances behavioral attraction (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: sNPFR signaling does not account for all changes induced by starvation in behavioral responses to a wider range of odor concentrations.
source: In our current study, however, we show that sNPFR signaling does not account for all changes induced by starvation in behavioral responses to a wider range of odor concentrations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on the behavioral data.

claim: Starvation leads to a decreased sensitivity in the Or85a ORNs, an odorant channel that mediates behavioral aversion.
source: Second, we show that starvation leads to a decreased sensitivity in the Or85a ORNs, an odorant channel that mediates behavioral aversion (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on the imaging data, with the functional role of Or85a supported by citation.

claim: DTKR signaling mediates the reduced sensitivity in the Or85a ORNs and partly accounts for enhanced behavioral attraction to high concentrations of vinegar.
source: Third, we show that DTKR signaling mediates the reduced sensitivity in the Or85a ORNs and partly accounts for enhanced behavioral attraction to high concentrations of vinegar.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on the imaging and behavioral data.

claim: Eliminating DTKR and sNPFR signaling pathways together fully reverses the effect of starvation on behavioral attraction across all odor concentrations tested.
source: Fourth, we show eliminating DTKR and sNPFR signaling pathways together fully reverses the effect of starvation on behavioral attraction across all odor concentrations tested.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on the double knockdown behavioral data.

claim: The same global insulin signal regulating sNPFR expression may also regulate DTKR expression.
source: Finally we show evidence suggesting that the same global insulin signal regulating sNPFR expression may also regulate DTKR expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the insulin signaling manipulation experiments.

claim: In the wild, rotten fruits early in the fermentation process are more attractive to Drosophila than fresh or highly fermented fruits.
source: In the wild, rotten fruits early in the fermentation process are more attractive to Drosophila than fresh or highly fermented fruits (Chakir et al., 1996; Castrezana and Markow, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the laboratory, well fed flies display very little attraction to apple cider vinegar.
source: In the laboratory, well fed flies display very little attraction to apple cider vinegar (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Behavioral attraction to higher odor concentrations of vinegar is the sum of the opposing effects of Or42b and Or85a.
source: In our working model, behavioral attraction to higher odor concentrations of vinegar is the sum of the opposing effects of Or42b and Or85a (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is a working model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: When flies face starvation, the balance of Or42b and Or85a inputs shifts to favor Or42b over Or85a inputs, as mediated by selective upregulation of sNPFR and DTKR in these ORNs, respectively.
source: When flies face starvation, the balance of these inputs shifts to favor Or42b over Or85a inputs, as mediated by selective upregulation of sNPFR and DTKR in these ORNs, respectively (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a working model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: The starvation-induced shift in Or42b and Or85a inputs could serve to encourage flies to risk ingestion of potentially toxic foods when under nutritional stress.
source: These processes could serve to encourage flies to risk ingestion of potentially toxic foods when under nutritional stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: sNPF shares structural and functional similarities with its vertebrate homolog, NPY.
source: sNPF shares structural and functional similarities with its vertebrate homolog, NPY (Hewes and Taghert, 2001; Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both sNPF and NPY show roles in controlling food intake and feeding behaviors in insects and vertebrates.
source: Both neuropeptides show roles in controlling food intake and feeding behaviors in insects and vertebrates.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about these neuropeptides.

claim: NPY is expressed in the vertebrate olfactory bulb and is thus positioned to shape olfactory processing during shifts in appetitive states.
source: Interestingly, NPY is also expressed in the vertebrate olfactory bulb (Hansel et al., 2001; Mathieu et al., 2002; Mousley et al., 2006) and is thus positioned to shape olfactory processing during shifts in appetitive states as well.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and includes an inference about its potential function.

claim: sNPF and NPF have been shown in the fly gustatory system to control sweet and bitter taste sensitivity, respectively, in parallel but opposing directions.
source: Indeed, sNPF and NPF, another NPY homolog in Drosophila, have been shown in the fly gustatory system to control sweet and bitter taste sensitivity, respectively, in parallel but opposing directions (Inagaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: DTK and DTKR share homology with substance P and its receptor NK1, respectively.
source: DTK and DTKR share homology with substance P and its receptor NK1, respectively (Li et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In rodents, emotional stressors cause long-lasting release of substance P to activate NK1 in the amygdala to generate anxiety-related behavior.
source: For example, in rodents, emotional stressors cause long-lasting release of substance P to activate NK1 in the amygdala to generate anxiety-related behavior (Ebner et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In Drosophila, DTK signaling has been shown to be critical for aggressive behaviors among male flies.
source: In Drosophila, DTK signaling has also been shown to be critical for aggressive behaviors among male flies (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Drosophila tachykinin mediates presynaptic inhibition in ORNs.
source: In previous work, we showed Drosophila tachykinin mediates presynaptic inhibition in ORNs and detected expression in the LNs (Ignell et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Starvation changes the perception of both attractive and aversive sensory inputs beginning at the peripheral nervous system.
source: Our results here resonate with discoveries in the gustatory system (Inagaki et al., 2014) and show that starvation changes the perception of both attractive and aversive sensory inputs beginning at the peripheral nervous system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings and comparison with previous work.

claim: Through the use of parallel neuromodulatory systems, the internal state of the organism functionally reconfigures early olfactory processing to optimize its detection of nutrients at the risk of ignoring potentially toxic food resources.
source: Through the use of parallel neuromodulatory systems, the internal state of the organism functionally reconfigures early olfactory processing to optimize its detection of nutrients at the risk of ignoring potentially toxic food resources.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Neuromodulatory systems likely also impact and reconfigure central circuits in appetitive contexts.
source: It is certainly likely that neuromodulatory systems also impact and reconfigure central circuits in appetitive contexts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential broader implications.

claim: Female flies that were 2–5 days old and presumed non-virgin were used for all experiments.
source: Female flies that were 2–5 days old and presumed non-virgin were used for all experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Flies were starved with water for 16–24 hr prior to experiments.
source: Flies were starved with water for 16–24 hr prior to experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: A fly was counted as having found the food when it spends 5 s or longer within a 5 mm radius of the center.
source: A fly was counted as having found the food when it spends 5 s or longer within a 5 mm radius of the center.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Antennae from 200 flies were collected for each condition for RNA-seq analysis.
source: Antennae from 200 flies were collected for each condition and total RNA was extracted using Trizol (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Over 80 million 36 bp reads were generated from two lanes for each of the biological conditions in the RNA-seq experiment.
source: For each of the biological conditions, over 80 million 36 bp reads were generated from two lanes.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: In total, over 136 million reads were mapped to protein-coding genes in the RNA-seq analysis.
source: In total, over 136 million reads were mapped to protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: sNPF peptide (AQRSPSLRLRF-NH2) was used at 98% purity.
source: sNPF peptide, AQRSPSLRLRF-NH2, 98% purity (Celtek Peptides, Franklin, TN) and DTK peptide, APTSSFIGMR-NH2, 98% purity (Bio Basic Inc., Markham, Ontario, Canada) were each dissolved in saline to a final concentration of 10 μM.
